title: Citta the teacher
hookLine: a householder who taught monks and debated wanderers (SN 41)

cards: A group of elder monks is back from the alms round, sitting together in a pavilion after their meal. They're discussing a question about the mind, and they don't agree. Some answer one way, some another.
A householder named Citta, in the next village on some business of his own, hears about it. He walks over, pays his respects, and asks: is it true you were discussing this? It is, they say.
He's a householder of the town of Macchikasanda. Not a monk. Today, his answer, and what the elders said to it.

teach.h: ARE THE FETTERS THE THINGS THEY BIND?
teach.b: First, the question. The fetter, and the things that can fetter, like the eye and what it sees: are they one thing under two names, or different things? Second, the picture.
A black ox and a white ox are tied together by a single yoke. Is the black ox the white ox's fetter? Is the white ox the black one's?
Neither, he says. The yoke is the fetter. In the same way, the eye isn't what binds forms, and forms aren't what binds the eye.
The desire and lust that arise between them, that's the fetter. Third, the praise.
The elders tell him it's his good fortune: he has the eye of wisdom that reaches into the Buddha's deep words. Fourth, the record.
That talk opens a whole chapter of the Samyutta given to Citta, where he questions monks, answers them, and talks with teachers of other schools.
And in the Anguttara's list of outstanding disciples, the Buddha names Citta of Macchikasanda as the foremost of his lay men who teach the Dhamma.
That's where this week has led: the women of the first sangha, then Anathapindika, who gave a grove and kept giving when he was poor, Jivaka, who gave medicine, and now Citta, who gave answers.

how: In Buddhist communities today, lay men and women also teach the Dhamma, lead study groups and meditation sessions, and give talks at temples and centers, alongside monks and nuns.

o: a monk who lives alone in the forest
a householder, living a lay life
a king's minister in charge of land

p: what really binds the eye and forms

s: he was a householder of Macchikasanda, not a monk.
the elder monks praised Citta's answer
they said he had the eye of wisdom reaching into the Buddha's deep words.
in Citta's picture, the black ox is the fetter
neither ox is: the yoke is.

games.q: you're Citta, a householder. you hear that the elder monks nearby are split on a question about the mind. what do you do?
o: stay out of it; it's monks' business.
go to them, ask about it, and offer an answer.
wait for the Buddha to settle it.
games.why: he goes, asks whether it's true, and answers with two oxen and a yoke. the elders tell him he has the eye of wisdom.

practice: No robe or title needed: think of one thing your own life has taught you well, how to calm a crying baby, how to get through a long shift, how to apologize.
Find the plainest picture for it, the way Citta found two oxen and one yoke, and hold it there for a few breaths.

wordCard.voice: Gahapati, householder. What Citta of Macchikasanda was, answering the elders with two oxen and a yoke, and named foremost of the lay teachers. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali gahapati: householder, the head of a household; the texts call him Citta the householder.

carryVoice: Your line: a householder teaches. The eye of wisdom didn't need a robe. Day seven hundred seventy, done.
